title: Human Reproduction & Development
description: Human reproduction from puberty to early childhood — sex hormones, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation, pregnancy, foetal development, birth, and infancy and childhood milestones.

notes.heading: 📌 Definition: Puberty and Sex Hormones
notes.body:
Puberty is the period of life when a child's body develops into an adult body capable of sexual reproduction. It is controlled by hormones released from the pituitary gland and the gonads: the testes in males and the ovaries in females.

In males, the testes produce testosterone. This hormone causes:

1. Growth of the penis and testes.
2. Sperm production beginning.
3. Growth of facial and body hair.
4. Deepening of the voice.
5. Increased muscle mass and broader shoulders.

In females, the ovaries produce oestrogen. This hormone causes:

1. Growth and development of breasts.
2. Widening of the hips.
3. Growth of pubic and underarm hair.
4. The start of the menstrual cycle (menarche).
5. Maturing of egg cells in the ovaries.

Both sexes experience a growth spurt during puberty. Changes in skin (more oil, sometimes acne) and emotions are also common. Puberty typically begins between ages 9 and 14 in girls and 10 and 15 in boys.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: Human reproduction and development involves hormonal changes, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation, pregnancy, birth, and childhood growth.

notes.heading: 🔑 How It Works: The Menstrual Cycle
notes.body:
The menstrual cycle prepares the female body for possible pregnancy each month. A typical cycle lasts about 28 days, although anywhere from 21 to 35 days can be normal.

The cycle has four main stages:

1. Menstruation (days 1–5): The thickened lining of the uterus breaks down and leaves the body through the vagina. This is called a period.

2. The uterus lining rebuilds (days 5–14): Oestrogen causes the lining of the uterus to thicken again, forming a spongy, blood-rich layer ready to receive a fertilised egg.

3. Ovulation (around day 14): A mature egg is released from one of the ovaries and travels into the oviduct. This is triggered by a sudden rise in luteinising hormone (LH).

4. The second half of the cycle (days 14–28): Progesterone keeps the uterus lining thick. If the egg is not fertilised, progesterone levels fall and the lining is shed, starting a new period.

If fertilisation occurs, progesterone remains high to maintain the lining during pregnancy.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: The menstrual cycle rebuilds and maintains the uterus lining in preparation for a possible pregnancy.

notes.heading: 🔑 Key Concept: Fertilisation and Implantation
notes.body:
Fertilisation happens when a male gamete (sperm) fuses with a female gamete (egg) to form a zygote.

During sexual intercourse, sperm are released in semen into the vagina. They swim through the cervix and uterus into the oviducts. If an egg is present in an oviduct, one sperm may penetrate its outer layer. The nuclei of the sperm and egg fuse, producing a zygote with 46 chromosomes — 23 from each parent.

Immediately after fertilisation, the egg membrane changes to prevent any other sperm from entering. This ensures the zygote has the correct diploid number of chromosomes.

The zygote begins to divide by mitosis as it moves slowly down the oviduct toward the uterus. By the time it reaches the uterus, it has become a ball of cells called an embryo. About 5–7 days after fertilisation, the embryo implants into the thickened lining of the uterus, where it will continue to develop.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: Fertilisation usually occurs in the oviduct; the embryo then travels to the uterus and implants in the lining.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example: Hormone Levels in the Menstrual Cycle
notes.body:
Worked example — reading a hormone graph across a 28-day menstrual cycle:

A graph shows the levels of FSH, LH, oestrogen, and progesterone. On day 14, one hormone shows a sharp peak.

Question: Which hormone peaks at day 14, and what event does it cause?

Answer: Luteinising hormone (LH) peaks sharply around day 14. This LH surge triggers ovulation — the release of a mature egg from the ovary.

Key points to read from the graph:

• FSH starts to rise at the beginning of the cycle and stimulates an egg to mature in the ovary.
• Oestrogen rises before ovulation and causes the uterus lining to thicken.
• LH spikes at day 14 and triggers ovulation.
• Progesterone rises after ovulation and maintains the uterus lining. If pregnancy does not occur, progesterone falls and the next period begins.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: FSH, LH, oestrogen, and progesterone work together to control the menstrual cycle.

notes.heading: 📎 Key Points to Remember: Pregnancy and Foetal Development
notes.body:
Pregnancy, also called gestation, lasts about 40 weeks in humans. It is usually divided into three trimesters.

First trimester (weeks 0–12):

• All major organs begin to form.
• The heart starts beating around week 6.
• The embryo becomes a foetus at about 8 weeks.
• The placenta and amniotic sac develop.

Second trimester (weeks 13–27):

• The foetus grows quickly and begins to move.
• Fingerprints form.
• Hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes begin to grow.
• The mother may feel the foetus move.

Third trimester (weeks 28–40):

• The foetus gains weight rapidly.
• Lungs mature in preparation for breathing air.
• The head usually turns downward, ready for birth.
• Fat is stored under the skin to help regulate temperature after birth.

Throughout pregnancy, the foetus depends on the placenta for oxygen, nutrients, and waste removal.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: Foetal development is divided into three trimesters, with major organs forming in the first trimester.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Common Mistake: The Placenta, Umbilical Cord and Amniotic Sac
notes.body:
Students often confuse three structures that support the developing foetus. Each has a different role:

Placenta — a disc-shaped organ that attaches to the wall of the uterus. It allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from the mother's blood to the foetal blood, and waste products such as carbon dioxide and urea to pass from the foetal blood to the mother's blood. The two blood supplies do NOT mix.

Umbilical cord — a flexible tube connecting the foetus to the placenta. It contains blood vessels that carry blood between the foetus and the placenta.

Amniotic sac — a fluid-filled bag that surrounds the foetus. The liquid inside is called amniotic fluid. It cushions the foetus against bumps, allows movement, and helps maintain a steady temperature.

Common mistake: thinking that the mother's and foetus's blood mix in the placenta. In fact, the blood supplies remain separate; substances cross between them by diffusion.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: The placenta, umbilical cord, and amniotic sac each support the foetus in a different way.

notes.heading: ✅ Check: Birth, Infancy and Childhood Development
notes.body:
Birth:

1. The cervix gradually opens (dilates).
2. The amniotic sac breaks, releasing fluid — often called the 'waters breaking'.
3. Strong contractions of the uterus wall push the baby through the cervix and out through the vagina.
4. After the baby is born, the placenta detaches from the uterus and is delivered as the afterbirth.

Infancy (birth to about 1 year):

• Babies grow rapidly and need milk for nutrition and antibodies.
• They develop reflexes such as sucking and grasping.
• They gain head control, roll over, sit, crawl, and may begin to walk.
• They begin to recognise faces and respond to sounds.

Childhood (about 1 year to puberty):

• Growth continues but is slower than in infancy.
• Motor skills improve: running, jumping, drawing, and writing.
• Teeth develop and are gradually replaced by adult teeth.
• Language and social skills develop quickly.

Development is fastest during infancy and slows during childhood until puberty begins again.

illustration.alt: Timeline of human reproduction and development from puberty through childhood.
illustration.caption: After birth, rapid growth and skill development occur during infancy and childhood.

flashcards.definition: The period of life when a child's body develops into an adult body capable of sexual reproduction, controlled by sex hormones.
flashcards.example: During puberty, boys produce testosterone and girls produce oestrogen, leading to secondary sexual characteristics.

flashcards.definition: The main male sex hormone produced by the testes. It triggers sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics.
flashcards.example: Testosterone causes the voice to deepen and facial hair to grow during male puberty.

flashcards.definition: The main female sex hormone produced by the ovaries. It controls the menstrual cycle and female secondary sexual characteristics.
flashcards.example: Oestrogen causes breast development and widens the hips during female puberty.

flashcards.definition: The monthly series of changes in the female reproductive system that prepares the body for a possible pregnancy.
flashcards.example: A typical menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days and includes menstruation, lining rebuilding, ovulation, and maintenance of the lining.

flashcards.definition: The release of a mature egg from an ovary, usually around day 14 of a 28-day menstrual cycle.
flashcards.example: Ovulation is triggered by a sudden surge in luteinising hormone (LH).

flashcards.definition: The monthly shedding of the thickened lining of the uterus through the vagina when no fertilised egg has implanted.
flashcards.example: Menstruation usually lasts about 3–7 days and marks the start of a new menstrual cycle.

flashcards.definition: The fusion of the nucleus of a sperm with the nucleus of an egg to form a zygote.
flashcards.example: Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct and produces a cell with 46 chromosomes.

flashcards.definition: The single cell formed when a sperm and egg fuse during fertilisation; it contains a full set of 46 chromosomes.
flashcards.example: The zygote divides by mitosis as it travels down the oviduct toward the uterus.

flashcards.definition: The process in which the developing embryo embeds into the thickened lining of the uterus.
flashcards.example: Implantation happens about 5–7 days after fertilisation.

flashcards.definition: A disc-shaped organ that develops in the uterus during pregnancy and allows exchange of substances between mother and foetus without their blood mixing.
flashcards.example: Oxygen and glucose diffuse from the mother's blood to the foetus across the placenta.

flashcards.definition: The period during which an embryo and then foetus develops inside the uterus; human pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks.
flashcards.example: Gestation is divided into three trimesters, each lasting about three months.

flashcards.definition: The liquid that fills the amniotic sac and surrounds the developing foetus, cushioning it from shocks and allowing movement.
flashcards.example: When the amniotic sac breaks before birth, it is often described as the 'waters breaking'.

questions.stem: Which hormone is mainly responsible for male changes during puberty, such as a deepening voice and facial hair growth?
questions.explanation: Testosterone is produced by the testes and is the main hormone responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics during puberty.

questions.stem: What event is triggered by a sudden peak in luteinising hormone (LH) around day 14 of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: The LH surge triggers ovulation, the release of a mature egg from one of the ovaries into the oviduct.

questions.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, on approximately which day does ovulation occur?
questions.explanation: Ovulation usually occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle, halfway through the cycle.

questions.stem: Where does fertilisation of the egg by a sperm normally take place in the female reproductive system?
questions.explanation: Sperm meet the egg in the oviduct. Fertilisation occurs there, and the zygote then travels to the uterus.

questions.stem: What is formed when the nuclei of a sperm and an egg fuse during fertilisation?
questions.explanation: The fertilised egg is called a zygote. It contains 46 chromosomes and begins to divide by mitosis as it moves toward the uterus.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes does a normal human zygote contain?
questions.explanation: A zygote is diploid, containing 46 chromosomes — 23 from the sperm and 23 from the egg.

questions.stem: What happens immediately after one sperm enters the egg during fertilisation?
choices: The egg membrane changes to block other sperm
The zygote implants in the uterus
questions.explanation: The egg membrane changes rapidly after fertilisation to prevent more than one sperm from entering, ensuring the correct chromosome number.

questions.stem: Which hormone is responsible for maintaining the thickened lining of the uterus during the second half of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: Progesterone rises after ovulation and maintains the uterus lining. If pregnancy occurs, it stays high; if not, it falls and the lining is shed.

questions.stem: Which statement about the placenta is correct?
choices: The mother's and foetus's blood mix freely in the placenta.
The placenta produces sperm for fertilisation.
The placenta allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from mother to foetus while keeping their blood separate.
The placenta stores food for the foetus to eat.
questions.explanation: The placenta is the site of exchange between maternal and foetal blood, but the two blood supplies do not mix. Substances cross by diffusion.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the amniotic sac and amniotic fluid?
choices: To carry blood between the foetus and the placenta
To cushion and protect the foetus from bumps and shocks
To digest food for the foetus
questions.explanation: The amniotic sac is filled with fluid that cushions the foetus, allows movement, and helps maintain a steady temperature.

questions.stem: During which trimester does the embryo become a foetus and do all major organs begin to form?
questions.explanation: The first trimester is when the major organs begin to form and the embryo is called a foetus from about 8 weeks onwards.

questions.stem: What is delivered from the uterus after the baby is born?
choices: The placenta, also called the afterbirth
questions.explanation: After the baby is born, the placenta detaches from the uterus wall and is delivered as the afterbirth.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical development during infancy (birth to about 1 year)?
choices: Gaining head control, rolling over, sitting, and crawling
questions.explanation: During infancy, babies develop motor skills such as head control, rolling, sitting, and crawling. Tooth loss and writing are childhood milestones, and voice deepening occurs in puberty.

choices: The release of the first egg
questions.explanation: Menarche is the first occurrence of menstruation, marking the beginning of the menstrual cycle during female puberty.

questions.stem: Which hormone causes the lining of the uterus to thicken before ovulation?
questions.explanation: Oestrogen rises during the first half of the cycle and causes the uterus lining to thicken in preparation for a possible fertilised egg.
